intro:
These exercises take the seven ZoKrates stages — write, compile, setup, compute-witness, generate-proof, export-verifier, verify — and force you to stop treating them as one opaque script. The work is operational rather than cryptographic: the cryptography lives inside ZoKrates, and your job in Rust is to shape proof-friendly inputs, drive the heavy stages from the right lane, keep witness material in custody, version every artifact, and translate a proof bundle into a verifier call without leaking anything the verifier should never see.

The through-line is custody and explicitness. A circuit ID, a key pair, a verification key baked into a deployed contract, and a witness on a prover worker are four different artifacts with four different secrecy levels and four different custodians. The exercises build toward a system where another engineer can read the manifest, see which version maps to which contract address, and operate the rollout safely — instead of inheriting a request handler that quietly pairs a fresh proof with a stale key.

exerciseSolutions.title: Split the ZoKrates workflow into build-time, release-time, and runtime responsibilities
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The single most useful observation about the seven stages is that they do not all belong in the same place, because they have genuinely different operational profiles: different frequency, different cost, different trust sensitivity, and different custodians. Forcing them into one script — a build.rs step or a request handler — collapses those differences and makes the system impossible to operate safely.

Classify the stages this way. compile is a build-time, source-control concern: it runs once per circuit version, deterministically, and produces a durable compiled program. setup is release-time and trust-sensitive: it runs once per circuit to derive a matched proving-key/verification-key pair, and because some schemes rely on a trusted ceremony, its provenance is part of your security model. export-verifier is also release-time: it emits a Solidity contract artifact once per circuit, which then enters ordinary deployment review. These three belong in a controlled admin CLI or CI lane, never in build.rs — they are too heavy, too stateful, and too security-sensitive to behave like ordinary compilation.

compute-witness and generate-proof are runtime, per-request work and belong in a proving worker, not a request handler. They are the only stages that touch the secret witness, and proof generation is expensive enough to be a queued worker job rather than a synchronous helper call. Treating proof generation like a tiny function inside a handler ties request latency to prover cost and puts witness material on the request path.

verify is the one stage that must stay verifier-side and witness-free. A verifier consumes only the proof and the public inputs; by construction it never receives the witness — that is the entire point of the proof. If witness material reached the verifier the zero-knowledge property would be meaningless, so verifier input must exclude it not as a precaution but as a definitional requirement.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Tagging each stage with its lane makes "this does not belong in build.rs" a property you can read off the type, not a convention.
criteria: compile, setup, compute-witness, generate-proof, export-verifier, and verify are each placed in a distinct lane (Admin, Prover, or Verifier).
compile, setup, and export-verifier are identified as once-per-circuit/release stages that must not run per request.
verify is kept verifier-side and witness-free, with the explanation that excluding the witness is definitional to zero-knowledge, not a precaution.

exerciseSolutions.title: Review a proof workflow for proof-friendly input modeling
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect here is treating the HTTP payload shape as the proof-program input shape. A ZoKrates circuit is not a general-purpose program: every operation it performs becomes constraints, and constraints are what make proving expensive. Raw JSON strings, variable-length lists, and unbounded notes fields all force the circuit to do parsing and bounds work it should never have to do, and they smuggle transport fields into the proof boundary by accident.

Normalize in Rust before witness generation. The fields the proof actually reasons about — the one public total and the one public limit the circuit must justify — should arrive as canonical, bounded, fixed-width numeric values. Rust parses the JSON, range-checks each amount, rejects anything out of bounds with a clear transport error, sums the list into a single field-sized total, and only then hands canonical numbers to compute-witness. The circuit sees two field elements, not a JSON document.

Large or irregular fields should become commitments or stay witness-only. The variable-length list of line items, for example, should not be fed item-by-item into the circuit; commit to it (a hash or Merkle root computed in Rust) and prove against the commitment, or keep the detail entirely witness-side. The unbounded notes field has no business in the proof at all — it is neither numeric nor relevant to the total/limit relationship, so it stays out of the circuit and out of the verifier input.

Which fields must never become public verifier inputs: any field that exists only because it was already in the HTTP payload. The verifier needs the public total and the public limit. It does not need the customer's raw JSON, the notes, or the individual line items. A field becoming a public input by accident — because it rode along in the DTO — is a leak of information the proof was supposed to hide. The contract that guards this needs reproducibility tests: a golden-vector test that pins a known input to a known canonical witness-argument vector and fails if the mapping drifts, plus a contract test asserting the set of public inputs is exactly {total, limit} across versions so an extra field can never slip in unnoticed.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Rust does the parsing, bounds, and summation; the circuit only ever sees two canonical field elements, and a contract test pins the public-input set so a transport field can never leak in.
criteria: The amounts list and limit are normalized in Rust (parsed, range-checked, summed into canonical u64 field values) before witness generation.
The variable-length line-item detail is committed to or kept witness-only, and the unbounded notes field is excluded from both circuit and verifier input.
A golden-vector reproducibility test and a public-input-set contract test are named to keep the mapping stable across versions.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design a versioned artifact manifest for proof generation and verification
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The design goal is custody clarity: every artifact should be attributable, versioned, and sorted into proving-side or verifying-side ownership. One mega-struct that does every job hides the custody model, so split the manifest into the parts that have different secrecy levels and different custodians.

Name at least four distinct artifacts explicitly: the compiled circuit, the proving key, the verification key, and the proof blob — plus the verifier contract reference (path before deploy, address after deploy). Each gets its own identity field rather than a shared anonymous path. The proving-side metadata (proving key ID, witness location) is access-controlled and must never appear in anything a verifier caller can read; the verifying-side metadata (verification key ID, contract address, the public-input shape) is publishable and ships with the deployment.

Versioning belongs on artifacts from the start, not after the first migration failure. A single circuit_version (or protocol/circuit-identity field like "age-check:v2") threads through both halves so that a proof, the key that produced it, and the contract that verifies it are all attributable to the same circuit revision. This is what makes a later mismatch detectable rather than silent.

The split below keeps proving-only fields (proving_key_id, witness retention) in ProvingManifest and verifier-facing fields (verification_key_id, contract address) in VerifierManifest, with the shared circuit_id and circuit_version on a small CircuitIdentity both reference. Retention and audit live as explicit fields — a proving key kept too long is a liability, a verification key is permanent because it is baked into the contract — so the policy is reviewable rather than tribal knowledge. The whole set is three small types, reviewable in one sitting.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Three small types: a shared CircuitIdentity, a secret ProvingManifest, and a publishable VerifierManifest — custody and version are visible in the type, not buried in one struct.
criteria: At least four artifacts are named explicitly: compiled program, proving key, verification key, proof blob, plus the verifier contract reference.
A circuit identity/version field (circuit_id + circuit_version) appears on a shared type both halves reference.
Proving-only fields (proving_key_id, witness_retention) are separated from verifier-facing fields (verification_key_id, contract_ref).
The set is three small reviewable types rather than one opaque mega-struct.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a verifier integration that leaks witness or mixes versions
exerciseSolutions.solution:
There are three distinct production defects here, and each has a precise fix.

First defect: witness exposure. The verifier-facing request type stores a witness_path next to the verifier request DTO. That field must disappear from the boundary immediately. The verifier consumes only the proof and the public inputs; the moment a witness path is reachable from a verifier request type, the boundary is too wide and the zero-knowledge guarantee is one careless log line away from being void. Remove witness_path (and anything witness-derived) from the verifier DTO entirely — not nulled, not optional, absent from the type.

Second defect: version selection from a mutable runtime config string. Choosing the verifier contract from a mutable string at runtime means a config edit can silently point proofs at the wrong contract. Replace it with an explicit, versioned mapping keyed by circuit identity: circuit_id + circuit_version maps to a specific contract address and verification key ID, resolved from an immutable published map, not a hot-editable string. The selected contract is then attributable to a circuit revision rather than to whatever the config happened to say.

Third defect: pairing a new proof blob with an older verification key. This is a contract failure, not a 'maybe verify and see' situation, and it must fail before any external verifier call or transaction submit. Add a preflight that asserts the proof's circuit identity, the verification key ID, and the target contract's expected key ID all agree. If they do not match, abort with a structured error — do not spend gas submitting a transaction that is guaranteed to revert. The failure path carries structured fields: circuit_id, circuit_version, expected verification_key_id, actual verification_key_id, and contract address, so an operator sees exactly which artifact drifted instead of a generic false.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: witness_path is gone from the type, the contract is resolved by circuit identity, and a structured preflight rejects key/version drift before any gas is spent.
criteria: witness_path is removed from the verifier-facing request type entirely.
Contract selection becomes an explicit, versioned mapping keyed by circuit identity instead of a mutable config string.
A preflight key/version-match check fails before any external verifier call or transaction submit.
The failure path carries structured fields: circuit_id, circuit_version, expected vs actual verification_key_id, and contract address.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design reproducibility and negative tests for the proof pipeline
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Proof failures are notoriously opaque: a verifier returning false tells you nothing about which of a dozen moving parts drifted. The cure is to test in layers and make every failure attributable to a specific artifact.

Pin artifact versions in CI fixtures. The compiled circuit, the proving/verification key pair, and a known-good proof for a known input are all checked in (or content-addressed and referenced by hash) so a refactor cannot silently change them. Each fixture carries the circuit identity (circuit_id + version) so a test can assert which revision it exercised. This is the reproducibility rule: tests run against pinned artifacts, and a fixture changing is a reviewed event, not a side effect.

Define at least two positive and two negative cases. Positive: (1) the canonical input produces a witness and a proof that native verify accepts; (2) a second valid input within bounds also verifies. Negative, each crafted to fail clearly: (1) wrong public inputs — a proof verified against public inputs it was not generated for must be rejected; (2) wrong verification key — verifying a v2 proof with the v1 key must fail; (3) wrong contract version — submitting to a contract deployed with a different vk must be caught by preflight before submission; (4) wrong witness — a witness that does not satisfy the constraints must fail at proof generation, not at verify. Each negative names the artifact that drifted, so the test failure reads 'v1 key rejected v2 proof' rather than 'verify returned false'.

Separate native verification from contract/deploy-path tests. A fast native verify (ZoKrates verify against the local verification key) is a good first CI gate: cheap, deterministic, and a strong signal the circuit and keys are internally consistent. But it is not the same as a deploy-path test. Native verify proves the proof system accepts the proof; it says nothing about whether the deployed Solidity verifier, its ABI encoding of public inputs, the gas budget, or the contract address mapping are correct. Those need a separate contract-level test (against a local chain or fork) that exercises the actual verifyTx call. Keeping the two layers distinct means a green native gate plus a red contract test points straight at the integration boundary rather than the cryptography.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Native-verify tests run against a pinned fixture and report the drifted artifact by name; contract/deploy-path tests (against a local chain) are kept as a separate layer.
criteria: At least two positive (canonical and second valid input) and two negative (wrong public inputs, wrong vk) workflow tests are defined.
Native verify tests are kept separate from contract/deploy-path tests, with the limits of native verify spelled out.
Pinned fixtures carrying circuit identity are named as the reproducibility rule.
Each negative case reports the specific drifted artifact, making failures attributable rather than generic.

exerciseSolutions.title: Plan audits, upgrades, and rollout for an Ethereum verifier integration
exerciseSolutions.solution:
An upgrade here is never one code deploy; it is an artifact and contract migration. The plan has to make trusted setup, verifier deployment, dual-version rollout, and ownership explicit before the first circuit change.

There are four distinct audit surfaces, owned by different reviewers. (1) Proving-scheme assumptions: if the scheme relies on a trusted setup, the provenance of that ceremony is part of the security model — who ran it, was the toxic waste destroyed, is the transcript published. (2) Circuit logic: does the .zok program actually encode the intended statement and its constraints, reviewed by someone who reads circuits. (3) Rust artifact custody: key access control, witness retention and purge, manifest versioning, and the boundary code that builds verifier requests. (4) Solidity verifier deployment: the generated contract still goes through normal Solidity review, gas analysis, and release discipline — being machine-generated by a ZK toolchain does not exempt it. These are reviewed independently because a flaw in any one of them voids the others.

Old and new verifier versions must coexist during rollout via dual verifiers. Deploy the v2 verifier contract alongside the still-live v1, keep both addresses published, and route by circuit identity: proofs tagged age-check:v1 go to the v1 contract, age-check:v2 to the v2 contract. Provers can be cut over gradually (canary a fraction of traffic onto v2) while v1 continues to serve in-flight and legacy proofs. Rollback is then boring: stop routing new traffic to v2 and point everything back at v1, with no contract redeploy required because v1 was never removed.

Publish the artifact-to-address mapping that operators and downstream consumers depend on: circuit_id + circuit_version maps to verifier contract address (and chain ID) plus the verification key ID it was deployed with. This is the single document that lets an operator confirm which proof goes to which contract, and lets a downstream consumer verify they are calling the right address. Gate promotion and trigger rollback on at least two rollout signals: verification failure rate on the new contract (a spike means inputs, encoding, or key pairing drifted), proving-queue age and witness build time (capacity regression), and contract-submit/RPC failure rate (gas, ABI, or chain issues). Promote v2 only when its verification failure rate matches or beats v1 over the canary window; roll back automatically if the failure or submit-error rate crosses a preset threshold.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A published circuit-identity-to-deployment map drives dual-version routing and canary status; a small signal gate decides promotion or rollback.
criteria: At least three distinct audit surfaces are named: proving-scheme assumptions, circuit logic, Rust artifact custody, and Solidity verifier deployment.
A dual-verifier rollout strategy lets v1 and v2 coexist, routed by circuit identity, with a boring rollback.
A published artifact-to-address mapping (circuit_id+version to contract address and vk_id) is included.
At least two rollout signals are named: verification failure rate, proving-queue age/witness build time, and contract-submit/RPC failure rate.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
contract = contracts/AgeCheckVerifier.sol
public inputs = 2
witness included = false
labSolution.explanation:
The starter code modeled the failure mode the chapter warns about: to_verification_request copied bundle.witness_path into the verifier-facing proof_path and set witness_included to true, leaving the contract empty and the public-input count at zero. That is exactly a leaky boundary — the witness is the secret the proof exists to hide, yet it was riding into the verifier request.

The fix maps only the verifier-facing fields. contract comes from bundle.verifier_contract, so it prints contracts/AgeCheckVerifier.sol. public_inputs_len is derived from bundle.public_inputs.len(), which is 2 for the ["45", "50"] vector. proof_path is copied from bundle.proof_path (the proof, not the witness), and witness_included is set to false because the witness_path is never read across the boundary. The ProofBundle still holds witness_path — the prover owns it — but to_verification_request simply does not consume it, which is why the compiler notes the field is unread and why the proof never leaks.

This is borrowing in service of a security boundary: to_verification_request takes &ProofBundle and clones out only the fields the verifier may see, so the witness stays in the prover's custody by construction. The three println! lines then print exactly the expected output: contract, public inputs = 2, and witness included = false.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should compile and setup usually live in different operational lanes from witness generation and proof generation?
reviewAnswers.answer: compile and setup run once per circuit version: compile produces a durable compiled program, and setup derives a trust-sensitive proving/verification key pair whose provenance is part of the security model. Witness generation and proof generation run once per request, touch the secret witness, and proof generation is expensive enough to be a queued worker job. Folding the infrequent, trust-sensitive admin stages into the same place as per-request prover work ties request latency to setup cost and puts heavy, stateful, security-sensitive steps on a hot path where they do not belong.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes a proof request different from a verifier request in Rust terms?
reviewAnswers.answer: A proof request carries the private witness and drives compute-witness and generate-proof on a prover worker, so its types legitimately hold witness material and proving-key references. A verifier request must be witness-free by construction: it carries only the contract reference, the public inputs, and the proof blob, because the verifier consumes nothing secret. In Rust this is a type-boundary distinction — the witness path should be reachable from proving-side types and absent from verifier-facing types entirely, so the zero-knowledge property cannot be lost to an accidental field copy.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is contract or key version drift often a bigger operational risk than one single failed proof?
reviewAnswers.answer: A single failed proof is a contained, observable event affecting one request. Version drift — a proof paired with the wrong verification key, or routed to a contract deployed from a different circuit revision — is a systemic mismatch that can fail silently, waste gas on transactions guaranteed to revert, or, worse, succeed against the wrong contract. It is a contract failure rather than a 'maybe verify and see' condition, so it should be caught by an explicit preflight before any verifier call; the most expensive ZoKrates mistakes are usually unmanaged version, key, and deployment boundaries, not one bad proof.

reviewAnswers.question: What does native verification prove, and what does it not prove about the Ethereum deployment path?
reviewAnswers.answer: Native verification (ZoKrates verify against the local verification key) proves the proof system itself accepts the proof for the given public inputs — that the circuit, keys, and proof are internally consistent. It is a fast, deterministic first CI gate. It does not prove anything about the deployed Solidity verifier: the ABI encoding of public inputs, the verifyTx call, gas budget, contract address mapping, and chain interaction are all untested by native verify, so the deploy path needs its own contract-level test against a local chain or fork.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should generated verifier contracts still go through normal Solidity review and release discipline?
reviewAnswers.answer: Being machine-generated by a ZK toolchain does not make a contract production-safe; export-verifier emits ordinary Solidity that is deployed, called, and paid for with real gas like any other contract. It still needs provenance, code and gas review, deployment review, versioned address mapping, and a rollback plan, because a flaw in the verifier deployment or its public-input encoding voids the guarantees of an otherwise-correct proof. Treating the generated artifact as exempt from release engineering is exactly how the deployment boundary becomes the place most mistakes happen.
